report.source_text: Direct examination showed numerous leukocytes and rare gram-negative bacilli (Figure 1C). Regular, grey, smooth colonies grew the next day. The oxidase test was positive for the 1-3 mm diameter, non-hemolytic colonies (Figure 1D&E), strongly suggesting that the isolated strain belonged to Pasteurella genus. The involvement of Pasteurella multocida was also strongly suggested here by mannitol fermentation (API-20E Array) (Figure 1F) and confirmed by MALDI TOF mass spectrometry.

report.source_text: Taking into account the animal contact and the short incubation period, suggesting the involvement of Pasteurella genus, an antibiotherapy associating amoxicillin 2 g tid and amoxicillin/clavulanate 2 g tid was administered intravenously, immediately after bacteriological sampling. No topical therapy was prescribed excepted for artificial tears. The outcome was favourable in the next three days (Figure 1G), allowing discharge of the patient with amoxicillin (2 g tid per os) alone once usual full sensitivity of Pasteurella multocida strain to amoxicillin was confirmed.

clinician.trajectory_summary: A 69-year-old man recently treated with chemotherapy was struck in the right eye by his dog, subsequently developing purulent conjunctivitis, peri-orbital edema, fever, and inability to open the eye. Physical exam showed signs of eyelid inflammation, skin rupture, and purulent encystment. Conjunctival secretions cultured Pasteurella multocida. CT imaging excluded intra-orbital involvement, supporting pre-septal cellulitis diagnosis. Intravenous amoxicillin/amoxicillin-clavulanate was started, followed by oral amoxicillin, resulting in favorable improvement within three days.
